entries.capture: Type '(?<source>.+?)' is not assignable to type '(?<target>.+?)'
entries.title: Type is not assignable to type
entries.explain: A value is stored somewhere (a variable, property or return) whose declared type does not accept it. TypeScript checks this when compiling so the mismatch cannot surface as a bug at run time.
causes: Assigning text to a number variable, often from input or the DOM, which give `string`.
Returning a value of a different type than the function's declared return type.
A possibly `undefined` value (`string | undefined`) stored where only `string` is allowed.
fix: Convert the value: `Number(text)`, `String(n)`.
Fix the declared type if it is the one that is wrong.
Handle `undefined` first, or give a fallback: `value ?? ""`.
entries.before:
let count: number = 0;
count = "5";   // TS2322
entries.after:
let count: number = 0;
count = Number("5");
entries.specific: A `{source}` is assigned where a `{target}` is required{onLine}.

entries.capture: Argument of type '(?<source>.+?)' is not assignable to parameter of type '(?<target>.+?)'
entries.title: Argument is not assignable to parameter
entries.explain: A function was called with an argument whose type does not fit the parameter's declared type.
causes: Passing a `string` to a `number` parameter, or the other way round.
Passing a value that may be `undefined` or `null` to a parameter that does not allow it.
Arguments in the wrong order, or an object missing a required property.
fix: Convert the argument (`Number(x)`), or check it for `undefined` first.
Check the parameter order and types (hover the function in the editor).
entries.before:
function double(n: number) { return n * 2; }
double("4");   // TS2345
entries.after:
function double(n: number) { return n * 2; }
double(4);
entries.specific: A `{source}` is passed where the parameter needs a `{target}`{onLine}.

entries.capture: Property '(?<prop>[^']+)' does not exist on type '(?<type>.+?)'
entries.title: Property does not exist on type
entries.explain: The type TypeScript knows for this value has no property with that name. TypeScript only allows members it can see in the type, even if the object might have more at run time.
causes: A typo or wrong casing.
The property belongs to a narrower type: for a union like `Cat | Dog`, only shared properties are allowed until you narrow it.
An object typed as `{}` or an interface that is missing the property.
fix: Fix the name, or add the property to the interface or type.
Narrow unions first: `if ("bark" in pet) pet.bark();`.

entries.capture: Property '(?<prop>[^']+)' does not exist on type '(?<type>.+?)'\. Did you mean '(?<suggestion>[^']+)'
entries.title: Property does not exist. Did you mean ...?
entries.explain: The property name does not exist on the type, but one with a very similar name does, so it is almost certainly a typo.
causes: A misspelling: `lenght`, `lenth`.
Wrong casing: `innerHtml` instead of `innerHTML`.
fix: Use the suggested name.
entries.before:
const word = "hello";
console.log(word.lenght);   // TS2551
entries.after:
const word = "hello";
console.log(word.length);
entries.specific: `{prop}` does not exist on `{type}`; you probably meant `{suggestion}`{onLine}.

entries.title: Cannot find name
entries.explain: Nothing with this name is declared or imported where it is used: no variable, function, class or type.
causes: A typo or different casing.
A variable declared inside a block or function and used outside it.
A missing `import`.
A Node or DOM global the project's type settings do not include.
fix: Check spelling against the declaration.
Declare it in the scope where it is used, or import it.

entries.capture: Cannot find name '(?<name>[^']+)'\. Did you mean '(?<suggestion>[^']+)'
entries.title: Cannot find name. Did you mean ...?
entries.explain: No declaration matches this name, but a similar one exists, so this is most likely a typo.
causes: A misspelled variable or function name.
Different casing (`Console` vs `console`).
fix: Use the suggested name.
entries.before:
const total = 10;
console.log(totl);   // TS2552
entries.after:
const total = 10;
console.log(total);
entries.specific: `{name}` is not defined; you probably meant `{suggestion}`{onLine}.

entries.title: Object is possibly 'null'
entries.explain: With `strictNullChecks`, TypeScript tracks values that may be `null`. This expression may be `null` here, and using a property on `null` throws at run time, so TypeScript stops you.
causes: Using the result of `document.querySelector` or `getElementById` directly: they return `null` when nothing matches.
`String.match()` returns `null` when there is no match.
A function declared to return `T | null`.
fix: Store the value and check it: `const el = ...; if (el) el.textContent = "hi";`.
Or use optional chaining: `match?.[1]`.
Use the `!` non-null assertion only when you are certain.
entries.before: document.querySelector("#title").textContent = "Hi";   // TS2531
entries.after:
const title = document.querySelector("#title");
if (title) title.textContent = "Hi";

entries.title: Object is possibly 'undefined'
entries.explain: This expression's type includes `undefined`, and using a property on `undefined` throws at run time. TypeScript wants proof it has a value first.
causes: Optional properties (`a?.b` returns `undefined` when `a` is missing; `obj.opt` where `opt?:`).
Array lookups such as `find()` that may find nothing.
Indexing with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` turned on.
fix: Check before use: `if (x !== undefined) ...`.
Use `?.` and `??`: `user.address?.city ?? "unknown"`.
entries.before:
const users = [{ name: "Ann" }];
console.log(users.find(u => u.name === "Bo").name);   // TS2532
entries.after:
const users = [{ name: "Ann" }];
console.log(users.find(u => u.name === "Bo")?.name ?? "not found");

entries.title: Variable is possibly 'null'
entries.explain: The variable's type includes `null` (for example `HTMLElement | null`), and the code uses it as if it always has a value. If it is `null` at run time, the property access throws.
causes: A DOM lookup (`querySelector`, `getElementById`) stored and then used without a check.
A `match()` result used without checking.
A variable declared as `T | null`.
fix: Check it: `if (el) { ... }` or `if (el === null) return;`; TypeScript then knows it is not `null`.
Or use `el?.textContent`.
entries.before:
const el = document.getElementById("out");
el.textContent = "done";   // TS18047
entries.after:
const el = document.getElementById("out");
if (el) el.textContent = "done";

entries.title: Variable is possibly 'undefined'
entries.explain: The variable's type includes `undefined`, and the code uses it as if it always has a value. If it is `undefined` at run time, the property access throws.
causes: The result of `array.find()`, which is `undefined` when nothing matches.
An optional parameter or property (`name?: string`).
A `Map.get()` result.
fix: Check it before use: `if (user) { ... }`.
Or provide a fallback: `user?.name ?? "guest"`.

entries.title: Variable is possibly 'null' or 'undefined'
entries.explain: The variable's type includes both `null` and `undefined`, and the code uses it without checking. Either would throw when a property is read.
causes: A value typed `T | null | undefined`, such as an optional field that can also be set to `null`.
fix: Check with `!= null`, which rules out both: `if (x != null) ...`.
Or use `x?.prop ?? fallback`.

entries.title: Expected N arguments, but got M
entries.explain: TypeScript checks that every call passes the number of arguments the function declares. Unlike plain JavaScript, missing or extra arguments are an error rather than silently becoming `undefined` or being ignored.
causes: Leaving out a required argument.
Passing an extra one.
The function's parameter list changed and a call was not updated.
fix: Pass the arguments the function declares.
Make a parameter optional (`name?: string`) or give it a default (`name = "guest"`) if it really is optional.
entries.before:
function greet(name: string, greeting: string) { return `${greeting}, ${name}`; }
greet("Ann");   // TS2554
entries.after:
function greet(name: string, greeting = "Hello") { return `${greeting}, ${name}`; }
greet("Ann");
entries.specific: The call{onLine} passes {got} arguments, but {expected} are expected.

entries.title: Parameter implicitly has an 'any' type
entries.explain: Under `strict` (`noImplicitAny`), every parameter needs a known type. This one has no annotation and TypeScript cannot infer one from context, so it would silently be `any`, which turns off checking.
causes: A function parameter without a type annotation.
A callback whose context does not provide types (for example, a function stored first and passed later).
fix: Annotate the parameter: `function square(n: number)`.
Write callbacks inline where the context types them: `items.map(x => x * 2)`.

entries.capture: Property '(?<prop>[^']+)' is missing in type '(?<source>.+?)' but required in type '(?<target>.+?)'
entries.title: Property is missing but required
entries.explain: An object is used where a type with a required property is expected, and the object does not have that property.
causes: An object literal that leaves out a required field.
A new required property was added to an interface.
A typo in the property name, so the right one is missing.
fix: Add the missing property.
Or mark it optional in the type (`email?: string`) if it may really be absent.
entries.before:
interface User { name: string; age: number }
const u: User = { name: "Ann" };   // TS2741
entries.after:
interface User { name: string; age: number }
const u: User = { name: "Ann", age: 30 };

entries.capture: missing the following properties from type '(?<target>.+?)': (?<props>.+)
entries.title: Type is missing the following properties
entries.explain: An object is used where a type expects several properties that the object lacks.
causes: An object literal with only some of the required fields.
Using a value of a different, smaller type (such as `{}` or an object from another API) in place of the expected one.
fix: Add the missing properties, or make them optional in the type.
If the value is a different type, convert or map it into the expected shape.
entries.before:
interface Point { x: number; y: number; z: number }
const p: Point = { x: 1 };   // TS2739
entries.after:
interface Point { x: number; y: number; z: number }
const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 0, z: 0 };

entries.capture: and '(?<prop>[^']+)' does not exist in type '(?<type>.+?)'
entries.title: Object literal may only specify known properties
entries.explain: When an object literal is written directly where a type is expected, TypeScript checks for extra properties. A property the type does not declare is usually a typo, so it is reported.
causes: A misspelled property name (`agee` instead of `age`).
A property that belongs to a different type.
The type is missing a property it should have.
fix: Fix the property name.
Or add the property to the type if it belongs there.
entries.before:
interface User { name: string; age: number }
const u: User = { name: "Ann", agee: 30 };   // TS2353
entries.after:
interface User { name: string; age: number }
const u: User = { name: "Ann", age: 30 };

entries.title: Function lacks ending return statement
entries.explain: The function declares a return type that does not include `undefined`, but some path reaches the end without a `return`. That path would return `undefined`.
causes: An `if` with a `return` but no `else` and nothing after it.
A `switch` without a `default` that returns.
A loop that may finish without returning.
fix: Add a final `return` for the remaining case.
Or `throw` if that case should never happen.
entries.specific: A path through the function{onLine} ends without a `return`.

entries.title: A function whose declared type is not void must return a value
entries.explain: The function declares a return type, such as `number`, but its body has no `return` with a value at all.
causes: Computing a result but forgetting `return`.
Using braces in an arrow function, which turns the expression into a block: `(x): number => { x * 2 }`.
fix: Add `return` before the result.
Or drop the braces in an arrow function: `(x: number): number => x * 2`.
entries.before: const double = (x: number): number => { x * 2 };   // TS2355
entries.after: const double = (x: number): number => x * 2;
entries.specific: The function{onLine} never returns a value.

entries.title: Token expected
entries.explain: The parser expected a particular symbol, such as `,`, `)` or `;`, at this point and found something else. The code cannot be read until the syntax is fixed.
causes: A missing comma between object properties or array items.
A missing closing bracket or parenthesis.
A typo that makes a keyword or operator unreadable.
fix: Add the symbol named in the message at the reported spot, or just before it.
Fix the first syntax error first: later ones are often caused by it.
entries.before: const user = { name: "Ann" age: 30 };   // TS1005: ',' expected
entries.after: const user = { name: "Ann", age: 30 };

entries.capture: Cannot assign to '(?<name>[^']+)' because it is a constant
entries.title: Cannot assign to a constant
entries.explain: A `const` binding cannot be pointed at a new value after it is declared. Note that `const` does not freeze the object itself: you can still change an array's items or an object's properties.
causes: Reassigning or incrementing a `const` variable (`count++`).
Using `const` for a loop counter.
fix: Declare it with `let` if it needs to change.
Or create a new `const` with a different name for the new value.
entries.before:
const total = 0;
total += 5;   // TS2588
entries.after:
let total = 0;
total += 5;

entries.capture: Cannot assign to '(?<name>[^']+)' because it is a read-only property
entries.title: Cannot assign to a read-only property
entries.explain: The property is declared `readonly` (or the object is `Readonly<T>` / `as const`), so it can be set only when the object is created.
causes: Changing a `readonly` field after construction.
Mutating an object declared `as const` or typed `Readonly<T>`.
Assigning to a built-in read-only property.
fix: Create a new object with the change: `const next = { ...point, x: 5 };`.
Or remove `readonly` if the property really should change.
entries.before:
const origin = { x: 0, y: 0 } as const;
origin.x = 5;   // TS2540
entries.after:
const origin = { x: 0, y: 0 } as const;
const moved = { ...origin, x: 5 };

entries.capture: variable '(?<name>[^']+)' (?:used before its declaration|is used before being assigned)
entries.title: Variable used before its declaration or assignment
entries.explain: `let` and `const` variables cannot be used before the line that declares them (TS2448), and a `let` without an initial value cannot be read before some path assigns it (TS2454). At run time, the first case would throw a `ReferenceError`.
causes: Lines in the wrong order.
A `let x: number;` that is assigned only inside an `if`.
fix: Move the declaration above its first use.
Give the variable a starting value: `let total = 0;`.
entries.before:
console.log(message);   // TS2448
const message = "hi";
entries.after:
const message = "hi";
console.log(message);
entries.specific: `{name}` is used{onLine} before it has a value.

entries.title: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable
entries.explain: A name can be declared with `let` or `const` only once per scope. Declaring it again would create a second variable with the same name, which is an error.
causes: Repeating `let` or `const` when you only meant to change the value.
Two files without `import`/`export`, which TypeScript treats as one shared global scope.
fix: Assign without the keyword (and use `let` so it can change).
Or rename one of them. Adding `export {}` makes a file its own module.
entries.before:
let score = 1;
let score = 2;   // TS2451
entries.after:
let score = 1;
score = 2;

entries.title: Property has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor
entries.explain: With `strictPropertyInitialization`, a class property whose type does not include `undefined` must get a value where it is declared or in the constructor. Otherwise it would start out as `undefined`.
causes: A property declared with a type but never set.
Setting it in a helper method that the constructor calls, which TypeScript does not follow.
fix: Initialize it: `name = "";`, or set it in the constructor.
Use a parameter property: `constructor(public name: string) {}`.
Or make it optional (`name?: string`) if it can be missing.

entries.title: No overload matches this call
entries.explain: The function has several signatures (overloads), and the arguments do not fit any of them. The full message lists why each overload was rejected; the last one is usually the most useful.
causes: An argument of the wrong type for every overload.
Mixing types in a call such as `concat`, `reduce` or `addEventListener`.
A callback whose parameter or return types do not match.
fix: Read the per-overload details under the error to see which argument is wrong.
Convert the argument, or add a type annotation so TypeScript picks the right overload (for `reduce`, type the initial value).
entries.before:
const ids: number[] = [1, 2];
const more = ids.concat("3");   // TS2769
entries.after:
const ids: number[] = [1, 2];
const more = ids.concat(Number("3"));
entries.specific: The arguments{onLine} do not fit any version of this function.

entries.title: Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive
entries.explain: A `// @ts-expect-error` comment says the next line has a type error. That line no longer has one, so the comment itself is reported; this keeps such comments from hiding real problems later.
causes: The error the comment was suppressing has been fixed.
The comment is above the wrong line.
fix: Delete the `// @ts-expect-error` comment.
If the error is on a different line, move the comment directly above it.
entries.before:
// @ts-expect-error
const n: number = 5;   // no error here, so TS2578
entries.after: const n: number = 5;
entries.specific: The `@ts-expect-error`{onLine} has no error to suppress.

entries.capture: expression of type '(?<key>.+?)' can't be used to index type '(?<type>.+?)'
entries.title: Element implicitly has an 'any' type: expression can't be used to index
entries.explain: The object's type has a fixed set of keys, and the index is a general `string` that could be anything. TypeScript cannot know which property type comes back, so under `strict` it refuses.
causes: Indexing an object with a `string` variable: `prices[name]`.
Looping with `for (const k in obj)`, where `k` is a plain `string`.
fix: Type the object as a dictionary: `const prices: Record<string, number> = {...}`.
Or narrow the key: `name as keyof typeof prices` (only when you know it is valid).
Or use a `Map<string, number>`.
entries.before:
const prices = { apple: 1, pear: 2 };
function price(name: string) { return prices[name]; }   // TS7053
entries.after:
const prices: Record<string, number> = { apple: 1, pear: 2 };
function price(name: string) { return prices[name]; }

entries.title: Cannot find module or its type declarations
entries.explain: The `import` names a module TypeScript cannot locate, either the package itself or its type definitions.
causes: The package is not installed.
The package ships no types: install the matching `@types/` package.
A wrong relative path (`./util` vs `../util`), or a typo.
fix: Check the path or package name.
Install the package, and its `@types/...` package if it has no built-in types.
Prefer built-in APIs when they do the job.
entries.before: import { sum } from "./maths";   // the file is ./math.ts
entries.after: import { sum } from "./math";

entries.title: 'await' is only allowed within async functions and at the top level of modules
entries.explain: `await` pauses until a promise settles, which is allowed only in an `async` function or at the top level of a module. This `await` is inside a normal function.
causes: Using `await` in a function not marked `async`.
Using `await` inside a callback (`forEach`, `map`, an event handler) that is not `async`.
fix: Mark the function `async` (its return type becomes `Promise<T>`) and `await` it where it is called.
In loops, prefer `for (const x of items) await f(x);` over `forEach`, which does not wait.
entries.specific: `await` is used{onLine} in a function that is not `async`.

entries.title: This comparison appears to be unintentional: the types have no overlap
entries.explain: The two sides of `===` or `!==` have types that can never be equal, so the comparison is always `false` (or always `true`). It is usually a bug, such as comparing a string with a number.
causes: Comparing text with a number: `input === 5`.
Comparing against a value outside a union: `status === "done"` when the type is `"open" | "closed"`.
TypeScript has already narrowed the variable, so this branch can never match.
fix: Convert one side: `Number(input) === 5`.
Fix the literal or the type so they can match.
entries.before:
const input: string = "5";
if (input === 5) console.log("five");   // TS2367
entries.after:
const input: string = "5";
if (Number(input) === 5) console.log("five");
entries.specific: A `{a}` is compared with a `{b}`{onLine}; they can never be equal.

entries.title: This expression is not callable
entries.explain: The code puts `()` after a value that is not a function. Its type has no call signatures, so there is nothing to call.
causes: Calling a property as if it were a method: `items.length()`.
A variable that shadows a function with the same name.
Calling a value that is a union where some members are not functions.
fix: Remove the `()` for properties: `items.length`.
Rename the variable that hides the function.
entries.before:
const items = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(items.length());   // TS2349
entries.after:
const items = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(items.length);
entries.specific: A value of type `{type}` is called like a function{onLine}.

entries.capture: Operator '(?<op>[^']+)' cannot be applied to types '(?<left>.+?)' and '(?<right>.+?)'
entries.title: Operator cannot be applied to these types
entries.explain: The operator does not make sense for this pair of types under TypeScript's rules, for example `>` between a `number` and a `string`, or `+` between a `number` and a `boolean`.
causes: Comparing a number with text from input or the DOM: `count > "10"`.
Adding values of unrelated types.
fix: Convert first: `count > Number(limit)`.
Make both sides the same type.
entries.before:
const limit = "10";
if (count > limit) console.log("over");   // TS2365
entries.after:
const limit = "10";
if (count > Number(limit)) console.log("over");

entries.title: Arithmetic operand must be of type number, bigint or enum
entries.explain: `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` and `**` work only on numbers (or `bigint` or enums). One side is a `string`, `Date` or other type; JavaScript would coerce it silently, which TypeScript treats as a mistake.
causes: Doing arithmetic on text from input or the DOM: `"5" * 2`.
Subtracting `Date` objects directly (use `.getTime()`).
fix: Convert explicitly: `Number(text) * 2`.
For dates: `end.getTime() - start.getTime()`.
entries.before:
const qty = "3";
const total = qty * 2;   // TS2362
entries.after:
const qty = "3";
const total = Number(qty) * 2;
entries.specific: An operand of the arithmetic{onLine} is not a number.

entries.title: Declared but its value is never read
entries.explain: With `noUnusedLocals` / `noUnusedParameters`, TypeScript reports variables, imports and parameters that are never used. Often harmless, but sometimes a sign you meant to use the value and used something else.
causes: A leftover variable or import from earlier code.
A typo that uses a different variable than the one you computed.
fix: Use the value or remove the declaration.
For a parameter you must accept but do not use, prefix it with `_` (`_event`).

entries.title: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
entries.explain: The code read or set a property on a value that is `undefined` or `null`, which have no properties. The part before `.prop` on that line is the value that is missing.
causes: An array index past the end (`items[items.length]`), or `find()` that found nothing.
A property that does not exist on the object, often from JSON with a different shape.
A variable declared but not yet assigned, or a function that did not `return`.
Types that claim a value is always present (for example an `as` cast or `!`), which hid the problem from the compiler.
fix: Log the object just before that line to see which part is missing.
Guard with optional chaining and a fallback: `user?.address?.city ?? "unknown"`.
Fix the source: check array bounds, check `find()` results.
entries.before:
const users = [{ name: "Ann" }];
console.log(users[1].name);   // users[1] is undefined
entries.after:
const users = [{ name: "Ann" }];
console.log(users[1]?.name ?? "no second user");
entries.specific: `.{prop}` is used on a value that is `{value}`{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: ... is not a function
entries.explain: The code called something with `()`, but at run time that value was not a function: it was `undefined`, a string, an object or something else.
causes: A typo in a method name, which is `undefined` in JavaScript.
Calling an array method on something that is not an array (`data.map` where `data` is an object or a JSON string).
A method that does not exist on that type, such as `list.push` on a `Set` (it is `add`).
A missing or wrong import, so the name refers to a module object or `undefined`.
fix: Log `typeof` the value to see what it really is.
Parse JSON text first: `JSON.parse(text)`; wrap single objects in an array if needed.
Check the method name in the docs for that type.
entries.before:
const data = '[1, 2, 3]';
const doubled = data.map(n => n * 2);   // data is a string
entries.after:
const data: number[] = JSON.parse('[1, 2, 3]');
const doubled = data.map(n => n * 2);
entries.specific: `{expr}` is not a function at the moment it is called{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: ... is not iterable
entries.explain: `for...of`, spread (`...x`) and array destructuring need an iterable value such as an array, string, `Map` or `Set`. This value is a plain object, a number, `undefined` or `null`.
causes: Looping over a plain object with `for...of` (objects are not iterable).
Spreading or destructuring `undefined`, for example a missing property.
A function returned a single value or nothing instead of an array.
fix: For objects, loop over `Object.keys(obj)`, `Object.values(obj)` or `Object.entries(obj)`.
Provide a fallback: `for (const x of items ?? [])`.
entries.before:
const ages = { ann: 30, bo: 25 };
for (const age of ages) console.log(age);
entries.after:
const ages = { ann: 30, bo: 25 };
for (const age of Object.values(ages)) console.log(age);
entries.specific: `{expr}` cannot be looped over or spread{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
entries.explain: A variable declared with `const` was given a new value at run time. `const` bindings can never be reassigned; TypeScript normally catches this as TS2588 before running.
causes: `count++` or `total += x` on a `const`.
Reusing a `const` loop variable in a classic `for (const i = 0; ...; i++)` loop.
fix: Use `let` for values that change.
In `for` loops with a counter, use `let i`.
entries.before: for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++) console.log(i);
entries.after: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) console.log(i);

entries.title: TypeError: a value is not the type the operation needs
entries.explain: At run time, an operation met a value of the wrong kind, such as calling a non-function or reading a property of `undefined`. The types TypeScript checked did not match what the value really was.
causes: Data from outside (JSON, input, `any`) with a different shape than its declared type.
Casts (`as`) or non-null assertions (`!`) that were not true.
Using a value before it was set.
fix: Read the message: it names the operation and the value.
Validate outside data before trusting its type, and avoid `as` and `!` unless you have checked.
entries.before:
const user = JSON.parse('{}') as { name: string };
console.log(user.name.toUpperCase());
entries.after:
const user = JSON.parse('{}') as { name?: string };
console.log(user.name?.toUpperCase() ?? "no name");

entries.title: ReferenceError: Cannot access before initialization
entries.explain: A `let`, `const` or `class` is known from the start of its scope, but cannot be used until its declaration line has run. Using it earlier lands in the "temporal dead zone" and throws.
causes: Using a variable above its declaration.
A function, called early, that reads a `const` declared further down the file.
Modules that import each other in a cycle.
fix: Move the declaration above the code that uses it.
Call functions only after the values they need are declared.
entries.specific: `{name}` is used{onLine} before its declaration has run.

entries.title: ReferenceError: ... is not defined
entries.explain: The running code used a name that does not exist anywhere in scope. TypeScript usually reports this as TS2304 at compile time, so at run time it often means a global that exists in browsers but not in Node (or the other way round).
causes: Browser globals in Node: `window`, `document`, `localStorage`.
Node-only names in ES modules, such as `require` or `__dirname`.
A typo in code that was not type-checked.
fix: Use what the runtime provides: in Node ES modules, `import` instead of `require`, and `import.meta.dirname` instead of `__dirname`.
Check spelling, and declare or import the name.
entries.before: const fs = require("fs");   // in an ES module
entries.after: import fs from "node:fs";
entries.specific: `{name}` does not exist at run time{onLine}.

entries.title: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
entries.explain: Every function call uses a slot on the call stack until it returns. A function kept calling itself (or two functions kept calling each other) without stopping, and the stack ran out.
causes: A recursive function with no base case, or one that is never reached.
A getter or setter that reads or writes its own property (`get name() { return this.name; }`).
Two functions that call each other endlessly.
fix: Add a base case that returns without recursing, and make sure each call moves toward it.
In accessors, use a separate backing field (`#name`).
Rewrite very deep recursion as a loop.

entries.title: SyntaxError in JSON.parse
entries.explain: `JSON.parse()` (or `response.json()`) was given text that is not valid JSON. JSON is stricter than JavaScript: double-quoted keys and strings only, no trailing commas, no comments, no `undefined`.
causes: The text is not JSON at all: an HTML error page (`Unexpected token '<'`), plain text, or an empty string (`Unexpected end of JSON input`).
Single quotes or unquoted keys: `{name: 'Ann'}`.
A trailing comma, or parsing something already parsed (`JSON.parse` of an object gives `"[object Object]" is not valid JSON`).
fix: Log the text before parsing to see what you actually received.
Create JSON with `JSON.stringify`, not by hand.
Wrap `JSON.parse` in `try`/`catch` for input you do not control, and check `response.ok` before `response.json()`.
entries.before: const user = JSON.parse("{name: 'Ann'}");
entries.after: const user = JSON.parse('{"name": "Ann"}');
